newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call money starts to return to normal levels.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call money starts to return to normal levels.

text.p: Dutch call money started to climb again in late Thursday trade after falling to unusually low levels on Tuesday ahead of Friday's expiry of the last three-monthly credit quota under the current system.
The Dutch central bank has previously announced that it will switch to a new set of money market instruments from Friday as part of preparations for Europe's single currency, the euro.

Call money rates had dropped to levels of around 1.50 percent bid on Tuesday but was back up to between 2.12 and 2.25 bid earlier on Thursday and had returned to more familar levels of around 3.06 percent bid by late afternoon.
Dealers said the new money market instruments, unveiled by the Dutch central bank earlier this week, are unlikely to have a big impact on money market rates when they take effect tomorrow.
"It only means we have to change how we think, as banks are no longer allowed to have a deficit (on their cash reserve account) at the central bank at the end of the day," he said.
Dealers said some market players may occasionally get caught out and be forced to borrow under the central bank's marginal advance facility, which was introduced at 4.5 percent.
The marginal advance facility is comparable to the German Lombard rate, which sets the ceiling for money market rates.
Dealers said Dutch money market participants would continue to focus on the special advances rate when they came to set rates for call money.
The Dutch central bank has left the rate for its new special advances pact, which will run for seven days from tomorrow, at an unchanged 2.90 percent.
Dealers said they were happy with the new marginal advance facility as it was a safety net in case market participants ran out of liquidity at the end of a trading day.
"It will cost you some money, but it is kind of reassuring that there is a possibility to obtain liquidity if the need is there," said one dealer.

He said the new system would be good training for money market dealers as it brought Dutch practice more into line with the rest of Europe with whom the Netherlands will utlimately share a common currency.
The fixed advances or secured loans rate will continue to set the floor for money market rates. The secured loans rate has been pegged at 2.50 percent since March.
The guilder was virtually unchanged against the mark at 112.4225 per 100 marks from 112.415 on Wednesday.
